Magkakaroon ng pansamantalang road closures at rerouting sa ilang pangunahing kalsada sa Maynila simula 2:00 ng madaling araw ng Linggo, bukas, Marso 22 para sa gaganaping Judiciary Fun Run.

Apektado ang kahabaan ng P. Faura mula Taft Avenue hanggang Roxas Boulevard, gayundin ang northbound at southbound lanes ng Roxas Boulevard mula Quirino Avenue hanggang P. Ocampo. Isasara rin ang bahagi ng Quirino Avenue, Kalaw Avenue, at P. Burgos Avenue.

Ipinatupad din ang rerouting scheme para sa mga motorista. Ang mga galing Bonifacio Drive na papuntang Roxas Boulevard southbound ay kailangang dumaan sa P. Burgos. Ang mga manggagaling naman sa Kalaw at Quirino ay idadaan sa mga alternatibong kalsada tulad ng Adriatico, M.H. del Pilar, at Taft Avenue.

Samantala, ang mga heavy vehicles mula Pasay na patungong northbound ng Roxas Boulevard ay papalihisin sa Quirino Avenue, habang maaaring gamitin ng light vehicles ang service road.

Magkakaroon din ng stop-and-go traffic sa ilang bahagi tulad ng Mabini at P. Faura.

Pinapayuhan ang mga motorista na maglaan ng dagdag na oras sa biyahe, sumunod sa traffic advisories, at kung maaari ay umiwas muna sa mga apektadong lugar upang maiwasan ang abala. | ulat ni EJ Lazaro

The Philippine peso has officially breached ₱60 per USD and is now at a humiliating all-time low—hitting ₱60.15 as shown in this screenshot from March 20 at 9:45 PM UTC (Morningstar data). This isn't just a blip; it's a national economic disaster unfolding live under weak leadership.

- The chart in the image tells the brutal story: In late February, the peso was still clinging to around ₱57.65. Over just a few weeks, it collapsed in a relentless upward climb on the USD chart (meaning peso freefall), surging past ₱58, ₱59, and finally smashing through the psychological ₱60 barrier. That's over 4% weakening in a month alone—historic lows hit multiple times this March, with intraday spikes as high as ₱60.40 before closing around ₱60.10–60.15 in recent sessions.

- The main trigger? Escalating geopolitical chaos in the Middle East, especially tensions involving Iran, which has driven global oil prices surging past $100 per barrel in spots. The Philippines imports nearly 100% of its crude oil—mostly from that volatile region—so skyrocketing prices explode our import bill, balloon the trade deficit, stoke inflation fears (record-high local fuel prices already biting), and hammer the peso downward. A globally stronger US dollar amid war uncertainty and Fed caution added fuel to the fire.

- But don't ignore the homegrown rot: Rampant corruption scandals, especially the massive flood control graft exposed since mid-2025 (billions siphoned through kickbacks up to 30%, ghost projects, padded contracts, and unbuilt infrastructure that cost taxpayers up to ₱118.5 billion or more). This has shattered investor confidence domestically and abroad—foreign and local capital flees or parks in cash/safe assets, FDI slows, public works stall, growth slumps to multi-year lows (like 4% in Q3 2025), and the peso stays vulnerable long-term. Research firms like ING warn the peso could remain weak through 2026 precisely because of these unresolved scandals eroding trust in governance.

- The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) intervened repeatedly in the forex market, dumping dollars to defend the currency and desperately try to hold it below ₱60. But those efforts crumbled under overwhelming external pressure plus the drag from lost confidence. No real buffers were built in time—despite clear warning signs for months.

- Most infuriating? President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself drew a personal red line back in January 2026: He explicitly said he "does NOT want" the peso to reach ₱60 because it would massively inflate our dollar-denominated debt payments and hurt the economy. He made it sound like a firm commitment. Well, Mr. President—here we are at ₱60.15 and beyond anyway. Your words rang hollow. Your administration failed spectacularly to prepare, protect, or even slow the slide—while the corruption mess you uncovered drags on without swift prosecutions, further tanking sentiment.

- Now ordinary Filipinos pay the price: Everything imported gets pricier overnight—fuel, food staples like rice, medicine, electronics, construction materials. Inflation will spike harder, jeepney and bus fares will jump, groceries will sting more, electricity bills will rise with oil-linked costs. OFW families sending remittances home will see those dollars buy fewer pesos while the cost of living explodes around them. Everyday life just got tougher for millions—no safety net in sight.

This is the bitter result of weak leadership presiding over a fragile, graft-riddled economy: No serious industrialization push, no strategic reserves or diversification to shield against global shocks, endless delays in holding the corrupt accountable—just photo-ops, dynastic games, and empty rhetoric while the currency bleeds out, investors run, and the people suffer.

Weak president + weak peso + unchecked corruption = a nation in deep pain.

The Marcos Jr. administration owns this failure lock, stock, and barrel. They had every opportunity to act decisively on graft, rebuild trust, and fortify the economy—they chose complacency and half-measures instead.

Time to wake up, Philippines. Demand real accountability and better leadership before it's too late.

#PesoAt60 #WeakLeadership #MarcosFailure #CorruptionCrisis #EconomicCrisisPH 🇵🇭💸
